title: The One Rule for Interview Data Structures

scenes.say: Every interview question boils down to one thing: how fast and how much space your solution uses. Why does Big-O notation matter so much?

scenes.label: Big-O
scenes.sub: Describes worst-case time or space as input grows
scenes.say: Big-O notation tells you how your algorithm scales as the input gets bigger. It’s the language of efficiency.
Arrays and hash maps are fast for access and lookup. Linked lists, trees, and graphs are flexible for connections and hierarchy.
Interview patterns use these structures: two pointers for arrays, hashing for lookups, depth-first and breadth-first for trees and graphs, and dynamic programming to optimize.

scenes.question: What’s the most common interview mistake?
scenes.right: Always state time and space complexity—O(n), O(log n), O(1)—for every solution.
scenes.say: The biggest trap? Not stating your algorithm’s complexity. Interviewers want to hear O of n, O of log n, or O of one for every solution.
